Executive Summary — Where Is Institutional Money Flowing?

Two lenses on the same question — where did money move this week, and across which markets (US, India, Global, Commodity)?

5.1 — Global: Macros, Commodities, US Stocks, US & Global ETFs

The big picture — Global
The Iran conflict escalated sharply this week rather than de-escalating, and nearly every global risk asset re-priced lower as a result. Brent surged past $100/bbl to ~$108 as the Houthis seized Yemen's port of Mocha, disrupting both the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea simultaneously — worse than last week's already-elevated $95-97 range. This drove a genuine "global bond meltdown" (traders' own description): US 10Y near 4.84-5.00%, Germany's 10Y at a 15+ year high, Japan's at levels last seen in 1996. US equities and ETFs both had their weakest week in this report's history — only 26% of US stocks and just 13% of US ETFs were positive. Global ETFs were similarly weak (12 of 47 positive), with uranium miners crashing hardest (-10.4%, -8.2%).

US Story's Weekly Comparison tabs show where the resilience actually sits: energy/refining names (Valero, HF Sinclair, Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66) extended their 4-week winning streak, now joined by oil-services and shipping-linked ETFs (Breakwave Tanker Shipping, US Oil Fund, US Brent Oil Fund) as consistent 2-week gainers. Travel/leisure names (Booking Holdings, again) remained on the losing side. A Fed decision next week carries ~72% market-implied odds of a rate hike following strong US producer price data — the single biggest near-term catalyst for whether this week's damage extends or partially reverses.

Read together: this was a "flight from duration and risk" week, not a rotation — bonds, growth equities, and most global ETFs all fell together as a worsening geopolitical shock and hawkish Fed repricing compounded. Energy and shipping-linked names were the only consistent beneficiaries, and even those gains reflect the same conflict driving losses everywhere else.

5.2 — India: Macros, Indices, Sectors, Stocks

The big picture — India
India's fifth straight down week, and this time the usual DII cushion weakened too. Nifty 50 fell 2.09% — its worst week yet in this five-week losing streak — while breadth turned even more negative (571 Adv/1,037 Dec, worse than last week's 681/918). Large Cap DMA50 breadth, which has been eroding for three weeks (69%→60%→43%), collapsed further to just 31% — the market's biggest, most liquid names are now clearly under sustained pressure, not experiencing a one-week wobble. The 52-week-high list shrank again (143→125 names). DII buying, the market's main support through this whole episode, slowed sharply this week (+₹6,420 Cr vs three prior weeks of +₹17-23k Cr records) even as FII selling continued (-₹1,795 Cr, a 4th straight negative week, though milder than last week's).

India's 10Y G-Sec crossing 7% for the first time in over three months — explicitly described by traders as part of a global bond meltdown, not an India-specific issue — is the connective thread across this week's India story: it explains the equity weakness, the rupee's reversal (first weekly loss in a month), and the softer DII buying pace all at once. Rate-sensitive sectors likely bore the brunt, consistent with large-cap financials and consumer names dominating the "negative all 4 weeks" list in the Weekly Comparison tab (HDFC Bank, SBI, Bharti Airtel newly added this week, HUL, Maruti, M&M, ITC, Nestlé, Asian Paints, Avenue Supermarkets).

Not everything was negative: One 97 (Paytm) has now joined the large-cap "positive all 4 weeks" list alongside DLF and Kotak Mahindra Bank from prior weeks — genuine relative-strength names holding up through a genuinely difficult month for the index.

Read together: the FII-vs-DII flows story that dominated the first month of this report has been overtaken by a bigger, global force — the same oil/yield shock hitting US and global markets is now the primary driver of India's weakness too, and even DII's remarkable buying streak is showing its first signs of fatigue against it.

Net read — where did the money move this week?
Out of: nearly everything with duration or growth-multiple risk — global bonds, US and global equities/ETFs broadly, India's large caps specifically, and (for the first time in a month) even the rupee. Into: energy and oil-services names specifically (US refiners, oil/shipping ETFs) as the one consistent beneficiary of the conflict driving everything else down; DII buying continued in India but at a much-reduced pace. The connective tissue: a worsening, unresolved Iran conflict (Hormuz + Red Sea now both disrupted) pushed oil past $100/bbl, which combined with a hawkish Fed repricing (72% hike odds next week) to drive a genuine global bond selloff — and that selloff, not FII/DII flows, is now the dominant force moving every market this report tracks.
01

FII / DII Cashflows

🔍 Analyst Take
DII's buying pace dropped sharply this week (+₹6,420 Cr, down from three straight weeks of +₹17-23k Cr records) while FII selling continued but also moderated (-₹1,795 Cr vs -₹5,613 Cr last week). The key change isn't direction, it's magnitude — DIIs pulling back their buying pace while the index kept falling (Section: India Story) suggests even domestic conviction is cooling, not just reacting to a one-off shock anymore. This is a more cautious setup than prior weeks — the reliable "DII absorbs everything" dynamic that supported the market for a month looks like it's fading rather than strengthening.

Reading the week
Both flows moderated together this week — FII selling eased (a positive sign, potentially the tail end of the Iran-shock-driven outflow) but DII buying eased even more sharply in percentage terms. With Nifty 50 down a 5th straight week (Section: India Story), the reduced DII support is notable — the market fell further this week despite less FII selling pressure than last week, suggesting the driver has shifted from flows to something else (see Debt Market and FX below).

02

FX Market — USD/INR

🔍 Analyst Take
The rupee's 3-week winning streak snapped this week (+1.35%, weakest since the FCNR inflow began supporting it) — and it weakened against every tracked currency, not just USD. This looks like the FCNR liquidity tailwind fading rather than a fresh shock, consistent with a calmer FII/DII week (Section 1) but a weaker equity market (India Story) — the rupee move and equity weakness likely share a common cause (see Debt Market). Exporters (IT, pharma) get a modest relief here after three weeks of headwind; import-sensitive names should watch whether this proves a one-week correction or a resumption of the pre-FCNR weakening trend.

Rupee context
As flagged last week, the FCNR(B)-driven rupee strength was a liquidity event, not a structural re-rating — this week's reversal is consistent with that tailwind fading as expected. The broad-based nature of the weakness (against JPY, GBP, EUR, AED, IDR all at once) suggests either renewed risk-off sentiment or a genuine resumption of underlying rupee pressure — worth cross-referencing against the Debt Market section below for whether yields are telling the same story.
03

Commodities — Weekly Snapshot

🔍 Analyst Take
Brent above $100/bbl (up from last week's $95-97) on a materially escalating conflict (Houthis seizing Yemen's Mocha port, Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea both now disrupted) is a genuine, worsening tail risk, not a one-week spike to fade. Energy-sensitive Indian sectors (aviation, paints, tyres, chemicals) face a second straight week of input-cost pressure with no resolution in sight — this is now a multi-week trend, not an isolated event. The consistent 4-week US refiner/energy strength (Valero, HF Sinclair, Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66 — see US Story Weekly Comparison) remains the cleanest way this report has identified to express the "oil stays elevated" view, though position sizing should account for how quickly this could reverse if there's any de-escalation news.

04

Debt Market

🔍 Analyst Take
India's 10Y crossing 7% for the first time in 3+ months, described by traders as part of a "global bond meltdown" (not an India-specific issue), is the single most important data point in this week's report — it directly explains the equity weakness (India Story), the rupee reversal (FX), and the softer DII buying (FII/DII) all at once. Rate-sensitive sectors (NBFCs, real estate, auto financing) face compounding pressure from both higher domestic yields and a hawkish Fed decision due next week (72% odds of a hike per markets). This is the clearest single signal to monitor into next week — a Fed hike confirmation would likely extend this pressure; a surprise hold could trigger meaningful relief across all the assets this yield spike has been weighing on.

What moved yields
Oil above $100/bbl (Commodities, above) directly raises India's import bill and inflation outlook, while producer price data in the US strengthened Fed rate-hike expectations for next week's meeting — both forces pushed yields up together globally, not just in India. A ₹10.49 trillion banking-system liquidity surplus provided some cushion against a sharper selloff, but wasn't enough to prevent the 3-month-high breach. With a Fed decision due next week carrying high hike odds, this yield pressure has a clear, near-term catalyst that could either extend or reverse it.

Executive Summary — India Story

Executive Summary — India Story
A fifth consecutive down week, and the worst one yet in this streak. Nifty 50 fell 2.09% and breadth deteriorated further (571 Adv/1,037 Dec vs last week's 681/918) — only 35% of tracked stocks advanced. The 52-week-high list continued shrinking (143→125), and DMA-based breadth confirms broad, deepening weakness: DMA50 crossovers were the worst yet (82 above vs 180 below, net -98), and Large Cap DMA50 breadth — which has been in freefall for three straight weeks (69%→60%→43%→31%) — is now the weakest reading of any cap bucket, a genuine reversal from earlier weeks when large caps were the market's most resilient segment. This lines up directly with India's 10Y G-Sec crossing 7% for the first time in 3+ months (Macros tab) — a global bond selloff, not an India-specific issue, appears to be the primary driver.

Market Breadth by Market Cap — DMA 50 / DMA 200

🔍 Analyst Take
Large Cap DMA50 breadth at 31% — down from 69% just three weeks ago — is the standout chart in this entire report. The "large caps as a safe harbor" thesis that held for the first month of this report has now fully broken down; every cap bucket is weak, but large caps have deteriorated fastest and furthest. DMA50 crossovers this week (82 above vs 180 below, net -98) are the worst reading yet — the below-DMA50 list is now large enough that it's less a stock-picking tool and more a confirmation that this is a broad market regime shift, not a rotation. The above-DMA50 list, by contrast, is a genuinely higher-conviction signal right now — crossing above a moving average against this much headwind means something.
Legend
Cap Bucket: Large = rank 1-100, Mid = 101-250, Small = 251-500, Micro = 501+ (re-ranked fresh each week by mcap). Breadth = % of stocks in that bucket trading above their 50-day / 200-day moving average.

Net effect
DMA200: 38 crossed above vs 68 below (net -30). DMA50: 82 crossed above vs 180 below (net -98, the worst reading yet). Both confirm the accelerating deterioration story from 4.1 — this is now a five-week trend, not a single bad week.
CMP

4-Week Comparison — India Stocks (mcap > ₹1,000 Cr)

🔍 Analyst Take
Consistent 4-week gainers now include a notable new large-cap addition: One 97 (Paytm) has joined Kotak Mahindra Bank and DLF as large-cap names positive every single week during this five-week downturn — a genuinely rare signal given how broad the selling has been. Meesho, Oil India and Welspun Corp round out the more liquid mid-cap consistent performers.

Consistent 4-week laggards have widened to include more mega-caps: Bharti Airtel and Avenue Supermarkets have joined the now-familiar cluster of HDFC Bank, SBI, HUL, Maruti Suzuki, M&M, ITC, Nestlé India, and Asian Paints — all negative every week for a month. This concentration in the largest, most liquid names is the clearest evidence yet that this is a systematic large-cap de-rating, not sector- or stock-specific weakness — worth distinguishing "quality on a month-long sale" from "a trend with further to run" based on your own read of when the global bond selloff (Macros tab) stabilizes.

Executive Summary — US Story

Executive Summary — US Story
The worst week yet for US assets in this report's history — a decisive risk-off move, not indecision. Only 248 of 948 stocks (26%) were positive, down sharply from last week's near-50/50 split. US ETFs were even weaker (580 of 4,388, 13% positive) — Fixed Income, Asset Allocation and Equity asset classes all posted negative averages, with only Commodity ETFs (+1.14% avg) holding up. This directly tracks the global bond selloff and oil surge detailed in the Macros tab. Energy/refining names (Valero, HF Sinclair, Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66) extended their multi-week winning streak — now the clearest, most durable theme this report has identified — while travel/leisure and medical-device names led the declines.
01

Top Performers — US Stocks

🔍 Analyst Take
Median return of -1.92% across 948 stocks confirms this was a genuinely bad week, not a mixed one. Electronic Components (+4.4% avg), Oil & Gas Integrated (+3.9%) and Semiconductors (+3.1%) were the bright spots; Insurance Brokers (-6.5% avg), Medical Devices (-5.9%) and Medical Instruments (-5.9%) were hit hardest — a pattern more consistent with rate-sensitivity and multiple-compression than any sector-specific news. This week's top-50 gainers carry an even higher median PE premium than last week (30.7x vs 23.1x market-wide) — in a week this broadly negative, paying up for the biggest % movers is riskier than usual, since a rising-tide effect isn't lifting the median stock at all.

Top Performers — US ETFs

🔍 Analyst Take
Median ETF return of -0.87% with Commodity the only positive asset class (+1.14% avg) is a clean read: commodity exposure was the one place to hide this week, directly tracking the oil surge in the Macros tab. Fixed Income's -0.65% average is itself notable — bonds normally cushion equity weakness, but this week's selloff was a bond-market-led event (Debt Market, Macros tab), so the usual stocks/bonds diversification benefit didn't work this week, a useful reminder that "flight to bonds" isn't automatic when bonds themselves are the source of stress.

4-Week Comparison — US Stocks

🔍 Analyst Take
The energy/refining theme keeps strengthening: Valero, HF Sinclair, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 all extended their positive streak, now joined this week by Apple (a genuinely different kind of name — mega-cap tech holding up during a broad selloff, worth noting as a possible flight-to-quality signal within tech) and two Brazilian names (Suzano, Itaú Unibanco). The refiner cohort remains the highest-conviction, best-aligned (fundamentals + technicals + macro thesis) call in this report.

Consistent laggards have gotten more severe, not just more numerous: Booking Holdings' 4-week losing streak deepened to a -10% week, joined by Howmet Aerospace (-11.4%) and Burlington Stores (-10.1%) as new severe decliners. Double-digit single-week declines within an already-established losing streak is a stronger warning sign than the streak alone — these look less like "quality on sale" and more like names with a deteriorating, not just paused, story.

2-Week Comparison — US ETFs

Executive Summary — ETF Weekly Comparison

The big picture
Oil and energy-linked ETFs are the clearest, most consistent 2-week theme in this entire report. Of 396 ETFs positive both weeks, the top of the list is dominated by oil/energy exposure: Breakwave Tanker Shipping (+18.5% then +43.9%), United States Oil Fund, United States Brent Oil Fund, and Invesco DB Oil/Energy Funds all gained meaningfully in both weeks tracked. This is a direct, clean expression of the Iran-conflict/oil-surge story running through the Macros and US Story tabs — these funds have now shown 2 straight weeks of strength backed by a clear, ongoing fundamental catalyst (not yet resolved). Digital assets (21Shares Polkadot Staking, +3.5% then +25.6%) also stand out, though that's a higher-volatility, less fundamentally-tied move.
🔍 Analyst Take
With only 2 weeks tracked, this list should be read as "confirmed direction, not yet confirmed durability." The oil/tanker-shipping cluster is the exception — it's backed by an active, worsening geopolitical catalyst (Macros tab), which gives more confidence than a typical 2-week momentum read would otherwise warrant. Broad Equity and Asset Allocation categories were overwhelmingly negative both weeks (see Top Performers — US ETFs tab for this week's specific breadth by asset class) — the "positive both weeks" list is a genuinely narrow, commodity/energy-concentrated pocket of strength within an otherwise weak 2-week stretch for US ETFs overall.

Executive Summary — Global Story

Executive Summary — Global Story
A sharply weaker week for Global ETFs — only 12 of 47 positive (26%), down from last week's 29 — as the escalating Iran conflict and global bond selloff hit nearly every region. Colombia (+3.49%) and Turkey (+3.16%) were the only notable gainers; uranium miners crashed hardest (Sprott Junior Uranium Miners -10.4%, Sprott Uranium Miners -8.2%), extending a pattern of extreme volatility in that specific niche. Latin America was the only region with a positive average (+0.33%), while Commodity-linked ETFs (-4.41% avg) and Global funds (-2.74% avg) were the weakest — notably, broad commodity ETFs fell even as oil itself surged, suggesting this basket is more diversified (including agriculture, metals) than a pure oil play. Across the two weeks now tracked for Weekly Comparison, only 7 of 47 ETFs have been positive both weeks — a narrowing list worth monitoring for a 3rd confirming week.
01

Global ETF Heatmap — Weekly Analysis

🔍 Analyst Take
Uranium miners crashing -10.4% and -8.2% in the same week that oil surged past $100/bbl is a notable divergence — nuclear/uranium sentiment decoupled from the broader energy complex this week, likely reflecting fund-specific or policy-related news rather than the macro conflict story. Avoid reading uranium-miner weakness as a signal about the broader commodity/energy theme — the US ETF comparison (US Story tab) shows oil-linked funds strengthening over the same period. Colombia and Turkey's gains are the only genuine bright spots this week and are too isolated (1-2 names each) to build a regional thesis around yet — watch whether they persist into a second week.

Executive Summary — Weekly Change

The big picture
Only 12 of 47 country/region ETFs were positive this week (25.5%), a sharp reversal from last week's 29/47 — consistent with the broad global risk-off move detailed in the Macros and US Story tabs. Latin America (+0.33% avg) was the only region to stay positive on average, while Commodity-linked ETFs (-4.41% avg) were the weakest despite oil's own strength — this basket includes broader commodities (agriculture, metals) that didn't share in oil's gains.

Weekly Comparison — Global ETFs

ETFs positive across all weeks tracked (2 of 2)
Colombia (+3.49% this week), UAE (+2.31%), Finland (+1.69%), Brazil (+0.87%) and 3 others — only 7 of 47 ETFs, down from 11 last week. This narrowing itself is informative: fewer names are showing sustained strength as the broader risk-off move deepens.
🔍 Analyst Take
Brazil dropping from last week's biggest gainer (+6.50%) to a modest +0.87% this week, while still remaining net-positive across both weeks, is a healthier pattern than an outright reversal — Brazil looks like it's consolidating gains rather than giving them back, worth distinguishing from names that flipped from positive to negative. Colombia and UAE being the most consistent performers both weeks, despite very different regional exposures (Latin America vs Middle East), suggests idiosyncratic, country-specific strength rather than a shared regional or thematic driver — treat each as its own case rather than assuming they're expressing the same trade.
